Product design case study · Concept project

Ledger AI helps freelancers see what their work is really worth.

I wanted Ledger to answer one question quickly: “After all the extra work, what did I actually earn per hour?”

RoleUX/UI Designer
Timeline4 weeks
ToolsFigma · FigJam · Forms
ScopeResearch → UI → Prototype

The challenge

A project can look profitable on paper while hidden revisions, meetings, and scope creep quietly push the real hourly rate down.

The design goal

Make profitability understandable in seconds, then let people explore the “why” through interaction.

MY DESIGN PRINCIPLE Show the answer first. Make the “why” one click away.

I kept coming back to this while designing Ledger. Freelancers should not have to decode a finance dashboard just to understand whether a project is going well.

01 · Problem

The “gross rate” can hide the real story.

A freelancer might invoice $10,000 for a project and still end up with a much lower effective hourly rate once the real workload is counted.

What the freelancer sees

$10,000 invoice · 80 estimated hours · $125/hr on paper.

What actually happened

Extra revisions, informal calls, messages, and unplanned work push the real rate down.

“I don't mind doing one small change. I mind when a lot of small changes quietly turn into hours of unpaid work.”Problem framing used for the concept
02 · Research framing

Start with the decision, not the dashboard.

I framed the concept around the moments where a freelancer needs clarity: understanding a falling rate, spotting scope creep, and deciding whether the next project is worth taking.

01

What am I actually earning per hour?

02

What is making this project less profitable?

03

What should I change before saying yes?

Who I designed for

A solo freelancer who is good at their craft but does not want their finance tool to become another job. They need the answer quickly, and the detail only when it matters.

“I don't want another dashboard to manage. I want something that tells me when my work has stopped being worth the time.”Product voice used to guide the concept
03 · Product direction

Design around one question: “Am I actually profitable?”

Instead of building another invoicing or accounting dashboard, I focused the experience on four moments of decision-making.

DECISION 01

True hourly rate first

Lead with the number that best represents the user's real outcome—not just revenue.

DECISION 02

Progressive disclosure

Keep the dashboard calm. Reveal the calculation only when the user asks “why?”.

DECISION 03

Explain scope creep

Show exactly where a project moved beyond the original estimate.

DECISION 04

Predict before it hurts

Warn users when a client or project is trending below their target rate.

DECISION 05

Help before saying yes

Estimate a fair project price from expected hours, revisions, and communication.

DECISION 06

AI stays contextual

No generic chatbot. AI connects signals, evidence, and an actionable next step.

A little more personal

I wanted Ledger to feel useful, not impressive.

I deliberately kept the interface quieter than most finance dashboards. The product should help you make a decision, then get out of the way.

01

No dashboard gymnastics

One primary number first. Supporting information earns its place by helping explain it.

02

Calm when the numbers are bad

Risk should be visible without making the product feel like it is scolding the freelancer.

03

AI should show its work

Recommendations point back to a signal the user can understand instead of asking them to trust a black box.

04 · Wireframes

Simplify first. Explain later.

The core architecture was built around a small set of questions instead of filling the screen with every possible metric.

[ TRUE HOURLY RATE ]
$87/hr
Target $120/hr

Revenue     $18.4K
Earnings    $12.5K
Unpaid time 35.5h

[ CLIENTS ]
Northstar     $148/hr
Acme          $112/hr
Nova           $76/hr
PixelCo        $49/hr

[ YOUR RATE ] 30D / 90D / 6M
Why this direction?

The first screen answers the highest-value question immediately. Everything else is secondary and can be explored on demand.

[ PROJECT ] Website Redesign
Estimated 32h → Actual 47.5h
+48% over estimate

Start ●──── Scope change ●──── Revision ●──── Today

Current rate $81/hr
Target rate  $120/hr
Why a timeline?

A timeline makes the moment of scope expansion visible, rather than forcing the user to reconstruct it from emails or notes.

05 · Final UI

A calmer finance product, built around one decisive metric.

These are the two screens I would lead with in the product: one explains where a project lost time, and the other makes client profitability easy to scan.

Screen 01

Project detail · make scope creep visible

Scope at a glance

The screen makes the gap between estimated and actual hours impossible to miss.

Timeline first

Scope changes are tied to moments in the project instead of buried in a report.

Calm by default

I wanted the interface to feel composed even when the numbers are not.

Screen 02

Clients · who is worth your time?

Simple ranking

Quiet hierarchy

At-risk, not alarmist

Warnings are visible without turning the product into a stressful red dashboard.

THE INTERACTION I CARE ABOUT MOST $87/hr → Why? → Where? → What should I do?

That simple drill-down is the heart of Ledger: headline number, explanation, evidence, then action.

06 · Prototype & validation

Test whether the interface makes the right answer obvious.

The prototype should be evaluated around short, realistic tasks: identify a risky client, understand a falling rate, and inspect why a project exceeded its estimate.

Task 01 · Find the risky client

“Which client is currently producing the weakest effective hourly rate?”

What to watch: can the user answer without opening multiple screens?

Task 02 · Explain the rate

“Why did this project fall below your target hourly rate?”

What to watch: can the user connect the headline metric to its causes?
Iteration 01

Clarify action labels so users know whether a button previews or immediately sends something.

Iteration 02

Replace internal product terminology with language freelancers naturally use.

Iteration 03

Increase emphasis on the gap between actual and target rates.

07 · Learnings

What changed in my thinking.

01

Simple beats complete

The product became stronger when the first screen answered one question well instead of showing every metric at once.

02

Numbers need context

An effective rate is useful only when the user can understand what caused it to move.

03

AI should earn its place

The strongest AI moments are evidence-based recommendations embedded directly into the workflow.

The product is not “AI that talks about your finances.” It is a system that continuously turns your freelance activity into a clearer picture of what your work is worth.
